July 1, 2013
OPINION 13-0112
90-A-1 P UBLIC FUNDS & CONTRACTS
La. Const. art. V , Sec. 31
Sheriff Robert Buckley
La. R.S. 13:5521
President, LA Sheriffs’ Association La. R.S. 13:5636
1175 Nicholson Drive
La. R.S. 13:5521, as amended in 2007, prevents an increase in salary
Baton Rouge, Louisiana 70802 for sheriffs absent legislation and does not require a reduction of
sheriffs’ salaries below that which was paid on June 30, 2010. It is
further our opinion that if a sheriff qualifies for the salary increase
authorized by La. R.S. 13:5636, he is eligible to receive the increase
based on the increase provided for the Orleans criminal court judges
Dear Sheriff Buckley:
granted by the legislature.
On behalf of the Louisiana Sheriffs’ Association, you have requested an opinion of this
office regarding the salary that is payable to Louisiana Sheriffs.
Prior to 2007, La. R.S. 33:1421 provided that sheriffs were to set their own salaries,
subject to a cap based on population of their respective parishes, with sheriffs in
parishes with populations above 400,000 being limited to the salary payable to the
judges of the Criminal District Court of Orleans Parish and sheriffs in parishes with
populations below 400,000 earning $20,000 less than the Orleans criminal court judges’
salaries.
Act 422 of the 2007 Regular Session of the Louisiana Legislature (“Act 422”) deleted
this salary scale by amending La. R.S. 33:1421(A)(1) to provide that “the rate of annual
compensation for all services required of sheriffs and ex-officio tax collectors of the
various parishes, including the Civil and Criminal Sheriffs for the Parish of Orleans may
only be increased by legislative act.” Act 422 further provided that this substantive
amendment was to become effective on July 1, 2010.
La. R.S. 33:1421 was subsequently redesignated as La. R.S. 13:5521 pursuant to Act
248 of the 2011 Regular Session of the Louisiana Legislature. The present day La.
R.S. 13:5521 provides the following with respect to the compensation rate of Louisiana
Sheriffs:
A.(1) The rate of annual compensation for all services required of sheriffs
and ex officio tax collectors of the various parishes, including the civil and
criminal sheriffs for the parish of Orleans, may only be increased by
legislative act.

Sheriff Robert Buckley
Opinion 13-0112
Page -2-
(2) Nothing in this Subsection shall mandate an additional appropriation
by the city of New Orleans.
(3) Repealed by Acts 1995, No. 525, §2, eff. Jan. 1, 1996.
B. In addition to the above salary, each individual sheriff shall be granted
ten percent of his annual compensation as an expense allowance.
C. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to limit a sheriff from
participation in an eligible deferred compensation program established in
accordance with 26 U.S.C. 457. A sheriff shall not authorize or receive an
employer contribution that would be more favorable than that offered to
the employees of the sheriff's office.
D. In addition to all other forms of compensation which are authorized for
sheriffs under the provisions of this Section, effective on July 1, 1999, the
annual compensation of each sheriff shall be increased by twelve
thousand dollars.
E. The compensation set forth in this Section shall not be changed by
amendment to this Section, or by other Act regardless of whether it
amends this Section, unless notice of intention to introduce the proposal
has been published on two separate days without cost to the state in the
official journal for the parish wherein the office is located. If the proposal
would change the compensation of all sheriffs in the state, publication
shall also be made in the official journal of the state. The last day of
publication shall be at least thirty days prior to introduction of the bill. The
notice shall state the amount of the change, the bill shall contain a recital
that the notice has been given, and certification of such publication shall
be attached to the bill.
In addition to the salary owed to sheriffs pursuant to La. R.S. 13:5521(A)(1), “each
individual sheriff shall be granted ten percent of his annual compensation as an
expense allowance. La. R.S. 13:5521(B). Furthermore, La. R.S. 13:5631-5636, which
were enacted by Act 350 of the 2012 Regular Session of the Louisiana Legislature to
establish the Louisiana Sheriff’s Executive Management Institute, provide that a sheriff
would also be eligible to receive a salary increase “up to the amount he is eligible to
receive as provided for in this Section” if he completes the training requirements
provided for in La. R.S. 13:5631-5636 and if “the legislature has established a salary
increase for, and appropriated funds for, salary increases for district court judges as
provided by law.” La. R.S. 13:5636(A).
In light of the background explained above, you have asked our office whether the
current sheriff’s salary structure is that which existed on June 30, 2010, and whether

Sheriff Robert Buckley
Opinion 13-0112
Page -3-
and to what extent a sheriff may be eligible for a salary increase based on an increase
in the salaries of Orleans criminal court judges granted by the legislature.
It is our understanding based on documentation you have provided to our office, that the
salaries paid to sheriffs on June 30, 2010, represent the last increase in a sheriff’s
salary which was tied to a raise granted to the judges of the Criminal District Court of
Orleans Parish. It is also our understanding that there have been no legislative acts to
increase a sheriff’s salary since that time. Therefore, if a sheriff is still in the same term
of office as he was in 2010, his salary is frozen at that level and cannot be reduced
during his term of office. See La. Const. art. V, Sec. 31, which provides that “[t]he
salary and retirement benefits of an attorney general, district attorney, sheriff, coroner,
or clerk of the district court shall not be diminished during the term of his office.” The
protection against reduction in salary these public officials are constitutionally entitled to
begin when the official qualified and was elected to office and not on the date the public
official takes office. See Avoyelles Parish Justice of the Peace, et al. v. Avoyelles
Parish Police Jury, 98-543 (La.App. 3 Cir. 6/23/99), 758 So. 2d 161, 167-168.
In response to your second question regarding whether and to what extent a sheriff may
be eligible for a salary increase based on an increase in the salaries of Orleans criminal
court judges granted by the legislature, we find it necessary to refer to the rules of
statutory construction. La. C.C. art. 13 requires that laws on the same subject matter
must be interpreted in reference to each other. When two laws relating to the same
subject matter exist, there is a presumption that the new law relating to particular
subject-matter was enacted with reference to former general law. Ryan v. Blount Bros.
Const., Inc., 40,845 (La.App. 2 Cir. 4/19/06), 927 So.2d 1242, 1259. Finally, it is “a
well-settled canon of statutory construction that the more specific statute controls over
the general statute.” State v. Sharp, 05-1046 (La.App. 1 Cir. 6/28/06), 939 So. 2d 418,
421.
The two laws we must consider in pari materia to answer your question are La. R.S.
13:5521(A)(1), which was amended by Act 248 and provides that the annual
compensation due to sheriffs “may only be increased by legislative act” and La. R.S.
13:5636, enacted in 2012, which provides that the sheriff may receive a salary increase
if he completes the training requirements provided for in La. R.S. 13:5631-5636 and if
“the legislature has established a salary increase for, and appropriated funds for, salary
increases for district court judges as provided by law.” La. R.S. 13:5636(A). We must
presume that the legislature was aware of the amendments made in 2007 to La. R.S.
13:5521(A)(1) when it enacted La. R.S. 13:5636 and thereby allowed sheriffs to receive
a pay increase upon completing certain training requirements, if the same salary
increase was permitted for district court judges by law. This pay raise is separate from
and in addition to a pay increase that would be granted for sheriffs by legislative act
pursuant to La. R.S. 13:5521(A)(1).

Sheriff Robert Buckley
Opinion 13-0112
Page -4-
In conclusion, it is the opinion of this office that La. R.S. 13:5521, as amended in 2007,
but effective July 1, 2010, prevents an increase in salary for sheriffs absent legislation
and freezes the sheriffs’ salaries to that level which was paid on June 30, 2010. It is
further our opinion that if a sheriff qualifies for a salary increase authorized by La. R.S.
13:5636, he is eligible to receive the increase based on the increase provided for the
Orleans criminal court judges granted by the legislature.
We trust this adequately responds to your request. However, if our office can be of
further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.
Yours very truly,
JAMES D. “BUDDY” CALDWELL
Attorney General

Our office received an opinion request from you submitted as counsel for the Louisiana
State Plumbing Board (“LSPB”) concerning whether the LSPB may offer continuing
professional education classes to licensed plumbers to fulfill the continuing education
requirement set by the LSPB.
As described in La. R.S. 37:1361(A):
The purpose of the legislature in enacting this Chapter is the protection of
the health, safety, environment, and general welfare of all those persons
who use and rely upon plumbing, and medical gas and vacuum systems
for their personal or commercial needs, and the affording to such persons
of an effective and practical protection against incompetent,
inexperienced, or unlawful acts by persons who perform plumbing and
medical gas and vacuum systems work. Further, the legislative intent is
that the State Plumbing Board shall be the sole and exclusive agency in
this state empowered to license natural persons and regulated business
entities engaged or seeking to engage in the business of plumbing and
medical gas and vacuum systems installation and verification and to
ensure compliance with the licensing requirements of this Chapter.
Nothing herein shall preclude any current authority of the State Licensing
Board for Contractors.
Consistent with the above described statute, the LSPB is authorized to formulate and
promulgate rules and regulations to govern the plumbing profession. Chapter 16 of Title
37 of the Revised Statutes addresses the rulemaking authority of the LSPB with respect
to continuing professional development, La. R.S. 37:1366(I) providing: “[t]he board may
establish and determine by rule minimum requirements relative to continuing
professional development for the renewal or reinstatement of any license or special

OPINION 13-0083

endorsement issued by the board.” The LSPB promulgated rules which establish a
program of continuing professional education (“CPE”), outlining specific CPE hours
which must be obtained by active plumbers seeking to renew a journeyman or master
plumber’s license (LAC 46:LV.1001),1 a water supply protection specialist endorsement
(LAC 46:LV.1003), and/or a medical gas piping installer or medical gas verifier license
(LAC 46:LV.1005).
In general, the rules describe: the number of CPE hours required for renewal;2 course
material which must be submitted to the LSPB annually for approval;3 course form and
content requirements;4 course provider requirements;5 and course instructor
requirements.6 Further, LAC 46:LV.1001(C)(10) specifically acknowledges the authority
of the LSPB to enter into a cooperative endeavor with certain groups to jointly provide
CPE services to licensed journeyman and master plumbers.7
The question submitted to this office for consideration in this opinion request is whether
the LSPB itself may offer CPE courses to fulfill the CPE requirements set and approved
by the LSPB. As described by La. R.S. 37:1361(A), the purpose behind the statutes
regulating the licensing of plumbers is the protection of the health, safety, environment
and general welfare of all persons who use and rely upon plumbing, and medical gas
and vacuum systems for personal or commercial needs, and to afford such persons an
effective and practical protection against incompetent, inexperienced, or unlawful acts
by persons who perform plumbing, and medical gas and vacuum systems work.
Further, as described by La. R.S. 37:1366(I), the legislature has specifically authorized
the LSPB to establish and determine minimum requirements relative to continuing
professional development of individuals who have received a license or special
endorsement issued by the LSPB. It would fit within this statutory authority for the
LSPB to provide CPE courses to fulfill CPE requirements set by the LSPB. Of course,
any classes sponsored by the LSPB would be subject to the substantive and procedural
requirements set forth in the rules promulgated by the LSPB, including the approval
process for providers of continuing education.
This conclusion is consistent with previous opinions issued by this office, where we
have stated the Louisiana Board of Examiners of Certified Shorthand Reporters may
sponsor continuing education courses (La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 10-0084) and the Board

Dear Ms. Ourso:
Our office has received your opinion request regarding the redistricting of the Iberville
Parish School Board as set forth in La. R.S. 17:63. Specifically, you ask whether the
School Board must comply with provisions of La. R.S. 17:63.
La. R.S. 17:63 states, in pertinent part: “The Iberville Parish School Board shall consist
of nine members. Eight members shall be elected from single-member districts and one
member shall be elected at-large. … No later than the deadline contained in R.S.
17:71.5, the Iberville Parish School Board shall develop a plan to provide for the eight
single-member districts. … Prior to the final adoption of the plan required in this
Subsection, the Iberville Parish School Board shall have a public hearing on the
proposed plan”.
La. R.S. 17:71.5(A) requires school boards reapportion based on the federal census by
December thirty-first of the second year after the census was submitted to the
President.
In conclusion, La. R.S. 17:63 is a validly enacted law and will remain effective unless or
until it is amended or repealed by the legislature or judicially declared unenforceable.
The Iberville Parish School Board should follow the legal requirements set forth in the
statute and create a redistricting plan consistent with the statute. This opinion is
consistent with Shelby County, Alabama v. Holder.1

OPINION 13-0075
90 – B – 4 – PUBLIC MEETINGS – State & Local Governing Bodies
Ms. Alison Miller
Executive Director La. Const. Art. XII, §3 La. R.S. 42:14
Vermillion Parish Tourist Commission
P.O. Box 1106 A public body may not utilize telephone conference calls during a
public meeting to obtain a quorum.
Abbeville, LA 70511-1106
Dear Ms. Miller:
Our office received your request for an opinion submitted on behalf of the Vermillion
Parish Tourist Commission (“Commission”). You have asked whether it is permissible
for a public body to utilize telephone conference calls during a public meeting to obtain
a quorum.
The right to observe the deliberations of public bodies, except in cases established by
law, is guaranteed by La. Const. art. XII, §3. The Open Meetings Law, La. R.S. 42:12 et
seq., describes and defines this constitutional right.
Our office has consistently opined that the Open Meetings Law requires that a quorum
of a public body be physically present at a meeting. La. Atty. Gen. Op. Nos. 99-385, 00-
423, 01-256, 02-0106 and 06-0311. Specific to voting, La. R.S. 42:14(C) requires that
all votes be made “viva voce.” Previous opinions have interpreted this “live voice”
requirement to require the person voting to be physically present, and further, that
appearance by telephone or video telephone does not satisfy this requirement. Id.
Thus, these opinions have stated that any participation by telephone, whether it is to
obtain a quorum or to allow voting by non-present members, is a violation of the Open
Meetings Law. La. Atty. Gen. Op. Nos. 01-256, 02-0106 and 06-0311.
This interpretation is consistent with the right to observe a public body’s deliberations.
Additionally, we note this interpretation is consistent when considering other state laws
which specifically address the use of telephone or video telephone in a meeting. By
way of example, consider the following:
Committee meetings between sessions; video conferencing
A legislative committee meeting that is held between sessions of the
legislature and during which no vote on any matter having the effect

OPINION 13-0075
Ms. Alison Miller
Page 2
of law is to be taken may be conducted by video conference. Each
house of the legislature may adopt rules of procedure to provide for and
accommodate committee meetings by video conference, including but not
limited to rules governing attendance and participation of members of the
legislature in and quorums of committees for such meetings. Such rules
shall provide for public participation in such meetings in accordance with
R.S. 42:11 et seq. For the purposes of this Section and any rules adopted
by either house of the legislature pursuant to this Section, "video
conference" shall mean a method of communication which enables
persons in different locations to participate in a meeting and to see,
hear, and otherwise communicate with each other. No committee
meeting shall be held pursuant to this Section unless a quorum of
the committee is present, in person, at the location at which the
meeting was advertised to take place.
La. R.S. 24:7 (Emphasis added).
Louisiana Medical Disclosure Panel; creation; membership; powers; duties
Notwithstanding the provisions of the Open Meetings Law, R.S. 42:11 et
seq., or any other law, if any member of the panel is physically present
at a meeting, any number of the other members of the panel may
attend the meeting by use of telephone conference call,
videoconferencing, or other similar telecommunication methods for
purposes of establishing a quorum or voting or for any other
meeting purpose allowing a panel member to fully participate in any
panel meeting. The provisions of this Subsection shall apply without
regard to the subject matter discussed or considered by the panel at the
meeting. A meeting held by telephone conference call,
videoconferencing, or other similar telecommunication method:
(1) Shall be subject to the notice requirements of R.S. 42:11 et seq.
(2) Shall not be held unless the notice of the meeting specifies the
location of the meeting at which a member of the panel will be physically
present.
(3) Shall be open to the public and audible to the public at the location
specified in the notice.
(4) Shall provide two-way audio communication between all panel
members attending the meeting during the entire meeting, and, if the two-
way audio communication link with any member attending the meeting is
disrupted at any time, the meeting shall not continue until the two-way
audio communication link is reestablished.
La. R.S. 40:1299.39.6(R) (Emphasis added).

OPINION 13-0075
Ms. Alison Miller
Page 3
Board of directors
The board of directors, or any committee of the board, may hold a meeting
by means of conference telephone, facsimile, or similar communications
equipment provided that all persons participating in the meeting can
communicate with each other. Participation in a meeting pursuant to this
Paragraph shall constitute presence in person at such meeting, except
where a person participates in the meeting for the express purpose of
objecting to the transaction of any business on the ground that the
meeting is not lawfully called or convened. The provisions of this
Paragraph shall not apply to any public body or any other entity
provided for in R.S. 42:13.
La. R.S. 12:224(E)(10) (Emphasis added).
Statutes such as the above, which authorize the use of telephone and/or video
conferencing, would not be necessary if this practice were generally permissible under
the Open Meetings Law. This is evident from the qualifying language in the above, i.e.,
La. R.S. 24:7 still requires that a quorum of the legislative committee be physically
present before any members of the committee may participate by video conference and
the language addressing the permissive use of telephones by a non-profit board of
directors in La. R.S. 12:224 specifically notes that it does not apply to any public body or
any other entity provided for in the definitions section of the Open Meetings Law (La.
R.S. 42:13).
In light of the above, it remains the opinion of this office that it is not permissible for a
public body to utilize telephone conference calls during a public meeting to obtain a
quorum.
We hope that this opinion has adequately addressed the legal issues you have raised.
If our office can be of any further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.
With best regards,
JAMES D. “BUDDY” CALDWELL
ATTORNEY GENERAL

OPINION 13-0061
90 - 1 - A – PUBLIC FUNDS & CONTRACTS
La. R.S. 46:1060
La.Const. art. VII, §14
Mr. Blake Kramer
The Franklin Parish Hospital Service District #1 may sell its accounts
Administrator receivable if such accounts are determined by the District to be
“uncollectible”. Should the district classify the accounts accordingly,
Franklin Medical Center
then such accounts should be sold to the highest bidder after giving
2106 Loop Road public notice and subject to the District receiving payment
commensurate with their value. Further, the District is not prohibited
Winnsboro, LA 71295
from selling the accounts in bulk, rather than one at a time, should
the District determine this method of sale would generate the most
interest and value.
Dear Mr. Kramer:
Our office received your request for an opinion submitted on behalf of the Board of
Commissioners for Franklin Parish Hospital Service District #1 (“District”) concerning
the sale of accounts receivable. Consistent with our discussion regarding your request,
the accounts at issue range in amounts from twenty dollars to around twenty thousand
dollars. Your request states that “all legal avenues have been exhausted” in pursuing
collection of these accounts, and that private corporate entities have expressed an
interest in the purchase of these accounts receivable.
In light of the above, you have specifically asked:
(1) Whether a political subdivision, such as the District, may sell accounts receivable
to a private entity;
(2) If the answer to the first question is in the affirmative, is the procedure for selling
accounts receivable the same as that which must be followed for selling surplus
movable property, i.e., declaration of surplus, publication, bid/auction, etc.; and
(3) If the answer to the second question is in the affirmative, can the accounts be
sold in a bulk transaction or must they be sold one account at a time?
As a starting point, we consider the ability of the District to dispose of property. The
powers of a hospital service district are described in La. R.S. 46:1060, which provides:
Any hospital service district thus created and named by any police jury or
any parish in the state shall constitute a body corporate in law with all the
powers of a corporation, shall have perpetual existence, shall have the

OPINION 13-0061
Mr. Blake Kramer
Page 2
power and right to incur debts and contract obligations, to sue and be
sued, and to do and perform any and all acts in its corporate capacity and
its corporate name necessary and proper for the carrying out of the
objects and purposes for which the hospital service district was created.
Such hospital service district shall have the right and power of
expropriating property for the purpose of acquiring land for any purpose
that it may find necessary in the operation of a hospital service district and
may require by donation or purchase, any existing hospital facility in the
district. It shall also have the power and authority to acquire any and all
necessary equipment and buildings for the purpose of performing the
objects for which it is formed, and shall own all sites and physical facilities
which are acquired either by donation, purchase, expropriation, exchange
and otherwise in full ownership.
Pursuant to La. R.S. 46:1060 a hospital service district is authorized “to do and perform
any and all acts in its corporate capacity and its corporate name necessary and proper
for the carrying out of the objects and purposes for which the hospital service district
was created.” Such acts would seem to include the sale of property or assets that are
determined by the District to be no longer needed for public purposes or which are
diminishing in value.
Your first question specifically asks whether it is permissible for the District to sell
accounts receivable, accounts which the District has claimed to have “exhausted all
legal avenues to collect.” In La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 02-0104, our office was asked
whether LSU Health Care Services Division could negotiate a sale of uncollected and
apparently uncollectible accounts receivable. LSU contracted with a commercial
collection agency who attempted without success to collect the accounts and LSU
Health Care Services Division then declared such accounts as “uncollectible.” Id. This
office concluded that we were unaware of any provision of law that would prohibit the
sale of such accounts “as long as the Health Care Services Division has exhausted all
reasonable avenues for the collection of these accounts and as long as the Health Care
services Division will receive payment for the accounts commensurate with their value.”1
Id.
Whether the accounts at issue in your opinion request should be qualified as
“uncollectible” or whether the District has exhausted all reasonable avenues for the
collection of such accounts is a fact specific inquiry, and our office does not serve as a
fact-finder. We do, however, note that before the District could contemplate the sale of
any accounts receivable, the District must give careful and deliberate consideration of
each specific account, including examining the District’s own efforts to collect on the
account. While your request states that the District has “exhausted all legal avenues to
collect” these past due accounts, your letter did not include a description of such efforts.
1 Please note that the requestor in La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 02-0104 indicated that “according to the
Accounting Principles Board, accounts that are more than six months old are worth fifty to sixty cents on
the dollar, while those that are more than one year old are worth about thirty cents on the dollar.”

OPINION 13-0061
Mr. Blake Kramer
Page 3
In considering the relationship between debts owed to a public body and La. Const. art.
VII, §14, our office has previously stated that this constitutional provision requires public
bodies exercise reasonable means to recover debts owed to the public body.2
Reasonable means must be determined by the agency on a case-by-case basis and on
sound business practices and principles.3 As described by La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 02-
0104, such reasonable means may include a public body entering into a professional
services contract with a third party for debt collection services.4
For the reasons described above, the District, and not our office, is in the best position
to consider what reasonable collection efforts should be undertaken by the District
before declaring the accounts “uncollectible” and, further, what amount would represent
a fair value for such accounts. However, consistent with La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 02-
0104, our office is of the opinion that there is nothing prohibiting the sale of
“uncollectible” accounts receivable provided prior reasonable efforts are made to collect
on such accounts, and the District receives payment for the accounts commensurate
with their value.
Should the District conclude that reasonable collection efforts have been made to
collect on the accounts receivable such that the accounts are properly classified as
“uncollectible,” the question then turns to the correct procedure for disposing of such
property.
As stated above, the revised statutes do not specify an exact procedure which a
hospital service district must follow in disposing of “uncollectible” accounts receivable.
However, pursuant to La.Const. art. VII, §14, the District should follow the same
publication and notice requirements that it would follow if it were disposing of surplus
movable property.5 Thus, the District should declare at a public meeting that the
accounts qualify as “uncollectible” and that the accounts will, after notice, be offered for
sale to the highest bidder. The District should fix a minimum price which would reflect
the fair value of the accounts and which may be obtained through an appraisal of the
accounts. Any sale must be such that the District receives payment for the accounts
commensurate with their value.
In response to your third question, we see nothing prohibiting the sale of the accounts in
bulk, rather than one account at a time, if such method is deemed by the District and the
District’s Director to be the method which would generate the most interest and income
for the property.
2
La. Atty. Gen. Op. Nos. 07-0067 and 05-0227.
3
La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 05-0112 and 03-0444.
4 See also La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 07-0067, 02-0188, 96-427.
5 See La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 93-391 (a hospital service district has the authority to sell surplus equipment
and must do so in accordance with La. R.S. 49:125 or at “public auction”) and La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 07-
0096 wherein we stated that “publication and notice allows opportunity for opposition to the proposed
action to be made known, and in our estimate, generates the most interest to get the best price for the
property sought to be sold.” Attached, please find copies of these opinions.

OPINION 13-0061
Mr. Blake Kramer
Page 4
In conclusion, it is the opinion of this office that the District may sell accounts receivable
to a private entity if such accounts are determined by the District to be “uncollectible” at
a public meeting. Should the district classify the accounts accordingly, then such
accounts should be sold to the highest bidder only after obtaining an appraisal of the
accounts representing their fair market value, setting a minimum price, and giving public
notice of the intended sale. Further, there is nothing which prohibits the District from
selling the accounts in bulk, rather than one at a time, should the District determine this
method of sale is the method which would generate the most interest and income.
We hope that this opinion has adequately addressed the legal issues you have raised.
If our office can be of any further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.
With best regards,
JAMES D. “BUDDY” CALDWELL

text:
July 25, 2013
Opinion 13-0038
Hon. Eugene Smith 160 TAXATION - Sales Tax
Mayor, Town of Arcadia
La. Rev. Stat. 47:303
P.O. Box 767
The Bienville Parish School Board is not entitled to a fee
Arcadia, LA 71001
or commission on taxes collected by the Department of
Public Safety.
Dear Mayor Smith:
Your opinion request has been assigned to me for research and reply. You have
asked for our opinion on a matter related to the collection of sales taxes.
According to your request, the Bienville Parish School Board (“Board”) serves as
the tax collection agency for Bienville Parish. Specifically, you ask the following
question: Since the Louisiana Department of Public Safety and Corrections
(“DPS”) collects the sales taxes on vehicle purchases for the Town of Arcadia, is
Arcadia obligated to pay the 1 ½% the Board charges for collecting sales taxes?
Our office addressed a similar question in Attorney General Opinion No. 05-
0348. There, we were asked by the St. Helena Parish Sheriff’s office whether the
Sheriff was entitled to commissions on the sales taxes remitted by DPS. In his
request, the Sheriff indicated that DPS remits the sales taxes collected on
vehicles to the political subdivision that imposed the tax. DPS then issues checks
made payable to the different political subdivisions and mails the checks to the
Sheriff as the central tax collector. The Sheriff deposits the monies into the sales
tax accounts, and at the end of the month, the Sheriff collects its commission and
issues checks to the different taxing bodies. The Sheriff asked for our opinion as
to whether he was entitled to commissions on the sales taxes remitted by DPS.
In our response, we recognized that the acts passed by the particular taxing
bodies at issue authorized the Sheriff to collect sales taxes on behalf of the
taxing bodies. The acts further provided that the Sheriff was to receive a fee or
commission on the sales taxes collected by the Sheriff. However, it was our
opinion that the vehicle tax was not collected by the Sheriff. Rather, the vehicle
tax was collected by DPS in accordance with its contracts with the taxing bodies,
and DPS then forwarded checks to the taxing bodies care of the Sheriff.
Therefore, it was our opinion that because the Sheriff did not collect the taxes
remitted by DPS, the Sheriff was not entitled to a fee or commission on those
taxes. La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 05-0348.

Opinion 13-0038
Hon. Eugene Smith
Page -2-
La. Rev. Stat. 47:303 governs the collection of sales and use tax on vehicles and
provides, in pertinent part, the following:
(B)(3)(b)(i) The vehicle commissioner and the governing body of
any political subdivision as defined in Article VI, Section 44(2) of the
Constitution of Louisiana, in which a sales or use tax has been
imposed by such political subdivision on the sale or use of motor
vehicles, shall enter into an agreement by which the vehicle
commissioner shall collect such tax on behalf of the political
subdivision. Except as provided in Paragraph (5) of this Subsection,
no certificate of title or vehicle registration license shall be issued
until such local tax is paid.
(ii) The tax imposed by the political subdivisions on the sale or use
of vehicles subject to the Vehicle Registration License Tax Law
(R.S. 47:451 et seq.) shall be collected by the vehicle
commissioner and distributed to the political subdivisions as
provided for in R.S. 47:301(10)(f) and (18)(b). The vehicle
commissioner shall withhold from any such taxes collected for the
political subdivisions one percent of the proceeds of the tax so
collected, which shall be used by the commissioner to pay the cost
of collecting and remitting the tax to the political subdivisions.
Our office has been provided a copy of the agreement referenced by La. Rev.
Stat. 47:303(B)(3)(b)(i) (“Agreement”). Our reading of the Agreement reveals that
it is executed by and between the Undersecretary of DPS on behalf of DPS and
the Vehicle Commissioner, and all the political subdivisions within Bienville
Parish, represented therein by the Board. The Agreement between the Board
and DPS provides that as compensation for its service and to pay the cost of
collecting and remitting the taxes, DPS is authorized to withhold from the taxes
collected one percent (1%) of the proceeds of the taxes so collected. DPS is
required to remit to the Board the proceeds, less this one percent (1%), each
month for distribution to the appropriate taxing jurisdictions within Bienville
Parish. The Agreement also requires DPS to post information that enables the
Board to distribute the proceeds to the appropriate taxing jurisdictions each
month.
In accord with Attorney General Opinion No. 05-0348, it is the opinion of this
office that because the Board does not collect the taxes remitted by DPS, the
Board is not entitled to the fee or commission for collecting those taxes as
provided by La. Rev. Stat. 47:303(B)(3)(b)(ii). Nevertheless, it is also our opinion
that the Board and Town of Arcadia are free to enter into an intergovernmental

Opinion 13-0038
Hon. Eugene Smith
Page -3-
agreement whereby the Board may charge a reasonable handling fee for
receiving payments from DPS.
We trust this adequately responds to your request. However, if our office can be
of further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.
Yours very truly,
JAMES D. “BUDDY” CALDWELL

title: Louisiana Attorney General Opinion 12-0086 (2013-08-07)
text:
August 7, 2013
Opinion 12-0086
Craig P. Petit, Fire Chief 90-A-1 PUBLIC FUNDS & CONTRACTS
La. Const. art. VII, Sec. 14
Luling Volunteer Fire Department
67 Anthony Street Public funds may be spent to provide food and non-alcoholic
beverages to volunteer firefighters during training sessions or
Luling, Louisiana 70070
workshops and during the response to an emergency or attending a
public relations event, provided the cost of the meal and beverages
are reasonable under the circumstances and proportionate to the
benefit received by the public.
Dear Chief Petit:
You have requested an opinion of this office regarding whether public funds may be
spent to provide meals and non-alcoholic beverages to volunteer firefighters in any of
the following circumstances:
(a) When volunteer firefighters attend local fire service related training lasting three or
more hours when the training occurs in the evenings or on weekends;
(b) When volunteer firefighters participate in a scheduled departmental work event
and/or workshop that is local and lasts three or more hours, most likely taking place on
weekends;
(c) When volunteer firefighters respond to an emergency incident that lasts for three or
more hours, starting with the time that the incident is dispatched and ending when the
apparatus and other equipment are placed back in service; or
(d) When volunteer firefighters participate in fire prevention and/or public relations
events (such as fire prevention visits to local schools) that last four or more hours.
By way of background, the public funds in question are proceeds from a 1/8 cent sales
and use tax levied in St. Charles Parish “to be dedicated and used to provide funds for
the purpose of giving fire protection to the property in said Parish, including but not
limited to constructing, maintaining and operating said Parish’s fire protection facilities
and paying the costs of obtaining water for fire protection purposes” . . . and “for the
purpose of acquiring buildings, machinery and equipment, including both real and
personal property in said Parish and for funding appropriate reserve funds in connection
therewith . . .” These funds are collected by the Parish and are transferred to the St.
Charles Firemen’s Association (“Association”) by contract between the two entities. In

Opinion 12-0086
Craig P. Petit
Page 2
exchange for the tax dollars, the Association agrees to provide fire protection to St.
Charles Parish.
Louisiana law provides that the proceeds of any special tax shall constitute a trust fund
to be used exclusively for the objects and purposes for which the tax was levied. La.
R.S. 39:704. Additionally, Louisiana jurisprudence provides that special tax
authorizations must be strictly construed. Police Jury of the Parish of Acadia v. All
Taxpayers, et al., 95-145 (La. App. 3 Cir. 3/29/95), 653 So.2d 94, rehearing denied;
Hemler v. Richland Parish School Board, 76 So. 585 (La. 1917); Watkins v. Ouachita
Parish School Board, 136 So. 591 (La. 1931); Hodnett v. Monroe City School Board,
277 So.2d 598 (La. App. 2 Cir. 1972) and Brock v. St. James Parish Council, 407 So.2d
1265 (La. App. 4 Cir. 1981), writ denied. It has consistently been the opinion of this
office that sales and use tax proceeds must be used solely for the purposes approved
by the voters. La. Atty. Gen. Op. Nos. 12-0089, 09-0150. You have not asked, and we
offer no opinion on, whether the particular tax proceeds in question may be used to
purchase food and beverages for volunteer firefighters. The opinion below focuses on
the use of public funds in general and is not specific to the tax proposition approved by
the voters.
Because your questions involve the expenditure of public funds, our response is
provided in light of La. Const. art. VII, Sec. 14, which generally prohibits public funds
from being gratuitously alienated, and provides as follows:
Section 14(A) Prohibited Uses. Except as otherwise provided by this
constitution, the funds, credit, property, or things of value of the state or of
any political subdivision shall not be loaned, pledged, or donated to or for
any person, association, or corporation, public or private ...
In order for an expenditure to be permissible under this constitutional provision, the
public entity spending the funds must have the legal authority to make the expenditure
and must show: (i) a public purpose for the expenditure or transfer that comports with
the governmental purpose for which the public entity has legal authority to pursue; (ii)
that the expenditure or transfer, taken as a whole, does not appear to be gratuitous; and
(iii) that the public entity has a demonstrable, objective, and reasonable expectation of
receiving at least equivalent value in exchange for the expenditure or transfer of public
funds. See Board of Directors of the Industrial Development Board of the City of
Gonzales, Louisiana, Inc. v. All Taxpayers, Property Owners, Citizens of the City of
Gonzales, et al., 2005-2298 (La. 9/6/06), 938 So.2d 11.
Our office has previously opined on the circumstances in which public funds may be
used to purchase food and beverages during work related training. In La. Atty. Gen.
Op. No. 03-0157, this office addressed whether public funds collected in St. John the
Baptist Parish could be used to provide volunteer firefighters meals, awards, and travel

Opinion 12-0086
Craig P. Petit
Page 3
expenses. With regard to whether meals could be provided for volunteer firefighters at
training programs or workshops, our office stated the following:
Clearly, in order for any fire department, and indeed many organizations,
to properly conduct business and communicate with and train personnel,
necessary and proper meetings, workshops and training programs are
appropriate. Such meetings, workshops and training sessions also clearly
serve the public purpose and create a public benefit of promoting proper
and efficient fire protection by the various volunteer fire departments. The
only remaining issue to be examined is whether the provision of meals at
such meetings, workshops and training sessions, as well as the cost
thereof, is proportionate to the public benefit the particular meeting,
workshop or training session serves.
La. Atty. Gen. Op. No. 03-0157.
The opinion ultimately concluded that it is the reasonableness of the expenditure under
the circumstances which controls. Thus, serving coffee or soft drinks, and perhaps a
moderately priced lunch or snacks, to firemen attending an all day workshop would
appear reasonable. The opinion further provides that serving reasonable meals to
volunteer firemen attending lunch time meetings scheduled to accommodate them at a
time when they are not otherwise required to be in attendance at their places of regular
employment would also seem reasonable. Id. Serving meals at brief meetings,
particularly meetings that could be scheduled at times other than meal times would
appear to be unreasonable. Id.
It remains our opinion that public funds may be utilized to educate and train public
officials and personnel with regard to their duties and responsibilities, including, in some
instances, providing meals during the training. Appropriate education and training
provided to a volunteer fire department clearly serves a public purpose and creates a
public benefit of promoting proper and efficient fire protection by the department and its
personnel. Public funds may be spent on food and non-alcoholic beverages to be
served to volunteer firefighters during training sessions or workshops when such
session or workshop is scheduled during normal mealtime and it is necessary to
conduct the training at that time. The cost of the meal must be reasonable under the
circumstances and must be proportionate to the benefit that the public receives. The
question of what type of food or drink is reasonable is a factual determination that our
office cannot make. We also caution you to consider the frequency of the training
sessions when determining whether to provide participants a meal. If training occurs on
a regular basis and is part of the firefighters normal working hours, it may be less
reasonable to use public funds to provide meals.

Opinion 12-0086
Craig P. Petit
Page 4
Your third scenario asks whether public funds may be spent to provide a meal to
volunteer firefighters who respond to an emergency incident that lasts for three or more
hours, starting with the time that the incident is dispatched and ending when the
apparatus and other equipment are placed back in service. Although responding to
emergency situations is part of a volunteer firefighters’ position, such events are
unscheduled and may occur at normal mealtimes, thereby not giving the firefighter the
option to make alternate plans. If responding to an emergency incident causes the
firefighter to miss what would otherwise be his mealtime, it may be reasonable and
therefore permissible to provide that firefighter with food. Although your question asks
about an emergency incident lasting three or more hours, we note that it is not the
length of the emergency that is determinative; rather, the totality of the circumstances
must be considered. Because of the number of different scenarios possible under this
question, we cannot provide you with a definite answer. You must review the facts on a
case-by-case basis in order to determine whether providing a meal would violate La.
Const. art. VII, Sec. 14.
The same holds true for your final scenario, where you ask whether meals can be
provided to volunteer firefighters when they must participate in fire prevention and/or
public relations events (such as fire prevention visits to local schools) that last four or
more hours. As stated above, you must review the facts on a case-by-case basis in
order to determine whether providing a meal would violate La. Const. art. VII, Sec. 14.
In conclusion, it is the opinion of this office that public funds may be spent on food and
non-alcoholic beverages to be served to volunteer firefighters during training sessions
or workshops when such session or workshop is scheduled during normal mealtime
hours and it is necessary to conduct the training at that time. The cost of the meal must
be reasonable under the circumstances and must be proportionate to the benefit
received by the public. Public funds may also be spent to provide food and beverage to
a volunteer firefighter who has to work through mealtime due to responding to an
emergency or attending a public relations event. Consideration should be given to the
reasonableness of the expenditure and whether it is proportionate to the public benefit it
provides.

Opinion 12-0086
Craig P. Petit
Page 5
We trust this adequately responds to your request. If you should have any questions
about the response contained herein, please feel free to contact our office.
Yours very truly,
JAMES D. “BUDDY” CALDWELL
ATTORNEY GENERAL

MICHAEL J. VALLAN
Assistant Attorney General

August 9, 2013
OPINION 13-0068
92-A-2-(b) RETIREMENT- Clerk of Courts
92-A-2-(g) RETIREMENT- State Employees
La. R.S. 11:411 La. R.S. 11:1503
La. R.S. 11:1511 La. R.S. 11:1512
Mr. Derek Ransome A court reporter who was formerly a member of the Clerks’ of
Court Retirement System and Relief Fund was correctly placed in
Director of Finance
the Louisiana State Employees’ Retirement System upon her
Nineteenth Judicial District Court rehire.
300 N. Blvd., Suite 3606
Baton Rouge, Louisiana 70801
Dear Mr. Ransome:
Our office received your request for an opinion on whether Ms. Charlotte Webre (“Ms.
Webre”) may rejoin and make contributions to the Clerks’ of Court Retirement System
and Relief Fund (“Clerks’ of Court Retirement System”).1 Your opinion request states
that Ms. Webre was employed as a court reporter by the Nineteenth Judicial District
Court from November 2, 1981, until October 15, 2000. During this time, Ms. Webre was
a member of the Clerks’ of Court Retirement System. Ms. Webre was subsequently
rehired as a court reporter with the Nineteenth Judicial District Court on September 1,
2004. Upon her rehire, Ms. Webre became a member of the Louisiana State
Employees’ Retirement System.2 Your opinion request letter indicates you contacted
the Clerks’ of Court Retirement System on behalf of Ms. Webre and asked whether she
was eligible to rejoin or renew her membership with their retirement system. The
Clerks’ of Court Retirement System responded that Ms. Webre could not rejoin their
retirement system because she did not meet the definition of “employee” under La. R.S.
11:1503 (4). You would like to know whether Ms. Webre should be allowed to rejoin
and make contributions to the Clerks’ of Court Retirement System.
The Clerks’ of Court Retirement System was established by Act 51 of the 1950
Louisiana Legislative Session. When Ms. Webre was initially hired by the Nineteenth
Judicial District Court, the Clerks’ of Court Retirement System included in its
membership the position of deputy clerk of court.3 Counsel for the Clerks’ of Court
1 See La. R.S. 11:1501 et seq.
2 See La. R.S. 11:401 et seq.
3 Act 51 of the 1950 Louisiana Legislative Session, Section 1 created a Clerks’ of Court Retirement
System for each Parish except Orleans Parish for the “Clerk of Court, deputies, and employees
throughout the State.” This act was codified in former La. R.S. 13:931. Act 421 of the 1964 Louisiana
Legislative Session amended and reenacted La. R.S. 13:931 and created a retirement system for each
Parish including Orleans Parish for “the clerks of the criminal and civil district courts, their deputies and

OPINION 13-0068
Mr. Derek Ransome
Page 2
Retirement System has informed our office that prior to 2001, it was common practice
for court reporters in East Baton Rouge Parish to be “deputized” so that they were
eligible to participate in the Clerks’ of Court Retirement System, even though they were
not employed by the clerk’s office. Your office has confirmed that Ms. Webre was in
fact sworn in as a deputy clerk during her initial employment with the Nineteenth Judicial
District Court. During her initial employment tenure, Ms. Webre was eligible to
participate in the Clerks’ of Court Retirement System because she was a deputy clerk.
Louisiana Revised Statute 11:1503 (4) was amended by Act 739 of the 2001 Louisiana
Legislative Session (“Act 739”), which removed the position of “deputy clerk” from the
definition of an employee entitled to participate in the Clerks’ of Court Retirement
System.4 However, the amendment allows any court reporter employed by either
Orleans Parish or East Baton Rouge Parish who was enrolled in the fund on or before
July 1, 2001, (the effective date of Act 739) to remain in the fund as a member. In
effect, Act 739 allows the court reporters in Orleans and East Baton Rouge Parish who
were participating in the Clerks’ of Court Retirement System as “deputy clerks” on or
before July 1, 2001 to remain in the system. Louisiana Revised Statute 11:1503 (4)
does not protect a member once they terminate their membership with the Clerks’ of
Court Retirement System.
Membership in the Clerks’ of Court Retirement System ceases when the member
“resigns, is dismissed, retires, or is otherwise separated from services as a clerk or
employee.”5 Based on the facts you have presented, Ms. Webre’s membership in the
Clerks’ of Court Retirement system ceased on October 15, 2000, when she left her
position as court reporter/deputy clerk with the Nineteenth Judicial District Court.
On Ms. Webre’s date of rehire, September 1, 2004, the Clerks’ of Court Retirement
System no longer allowed deputy clerks to be members of its retirement system.6 Upon
rehire, Ms. Webre was correctly placed in the Louisiana State Employees’ Retirement
System, which requires that “each person who becomes an employee in the state
service…shall become a member of the system as a condition of employment.”7
employees and the minute clerks and stenographers or reporters of the criminal and civil district courts of
Orleans Parish….” La. R.S. 13:931-13:960.2 were redesignated into Title 11 by Act 74 of the 1991
Louisiana Legislative Session.
4
La. R.S. 11:1503 (4) defines the word “employee” for purposes of the Clerks’ of Court Retirement and
Relief Fund to mean:
any regular employee of a clerk, minute clerk, and employees of the Louisiana Clerks of
Court Association, the Louisiana Clerks’ of Court Retirement and Relief Fund, and the
Louisiana Clerks of Court Insurance Fund, who works more than an average of twenty
hours per week. Any court reporter employed by either Orleans Parish or East baton
Rouge Parish who was enrolled in the fund on or before July 1, 2001, shall be allowed to
remain in the fund as a member or active member of the fund and to become eligible to
receive retirement benefits as required by law.
5 La. R.S. 11:1512.
6 La. R.S. 11:1511 and La. R.S. 11:1503 (4).
7 La. R.S. 11:411.

OPINION 13-0068
Mr. Derek Ransome
Page 3
In conclusion, it is the opinion of our office that Ms. Webre is not eligible to rejoin the
Clerks’ of Court Retirement System. We hope that this opinion has adequately
addressed the legal issues you have raised. If our office can be of any further

August 9, 2013
OPINION 13-0043
90 – B – 4 – PUBLIC MEETINGS – State & Local Governing
Honorable Herbert B. Dixon
Bodies
State Representative, District 26
La. R.S. 42:11 et seq.
804 Broadway Avenue
Alexandria, LA 71302 The Rapides Primary Health Care Center, Inc., a federally
qualified health care center and nonprofit corporation, is not
required to comply with the Open Meetings Law.
Dear Representative Dixon:
Our office received an opinion request from you concerning the applicability of the Open
Meetings Law, La. R.S. 42:11 et seq., to the Rapides Primary Health Care Center, Inc.
(“Health Care Center”), a non-profit corporation and a federally qualified community
health care center that provides health care to area residents, particularly those who are
economically disadvantaged. From facts available in the 2012 report submitted to the
Louisiana Legislative Auditor, we note that the Health Care Center was incorporated on
May 19, 1992 and organized to provide efficient and effective health care meeting the
medical needs of the community it serves, which is Central Louisiana.1 Further, we
understand that operations for the Health Care Center are funded through restricted
grants from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and other grants and
contracts are received from state and local government agencies.2
The Louisiana Constitution protects the right to observe the deliberations of public
bodies, except in cases established by law. La. Const. art. XII, §3. The public policy
behind requiring open meetings for public bodies is described in La. R.S. 42:12(A),
which provides:
It is essential to the maintenance of a democratic society that public
business be performed in an open and public manner and that the citizens
be advised of and aware of the performance of public officials and the
deliberations and decisions that go into the making of public policy.
Toward this end, the provisions of this Chapter shall be construed liberally.
Consistent with this statement, La. R.S. 42:14(A) requires that every meeting of a public
body shall be open to the public unless closed pursuant to exceptions provided for
within the Open Meetings Law. A “public body” for the purposes of the Open Meetings
Law means:
1http://app1.lla.state.la.us/PublicReports.nsf/3E6AED96A674972286257AA0006EEFAC/$FILE/0002D32A
.pdf. Accessed on July 17, 2013.
2
Id.

OPINION 13-0043
Representative Herbert B. Dixon
Page No. 2
village, town, and city governing authorities; parish governing authorities;
school boards and boards of levee and port commissioners; boards of
publicly operated utilities; planning, zoning, and airport commissions; and
any other state, parish, municipal, or special district boards, commissions,
or authorities, and those of any political subdivision thereof, where such
body possesses policy making, advisory, or administrative functions,
including any committee or subcommittee of any of these bodies
enumerated in this paragraph.
As represented in your opinion request, the Health Care Center is a non-profit
corporation. As an initial matter, it is clear that it is not a public entity, but rather a
private entity. The Louisiana Supreme Court has held that in order for an entity to be
considered public, the following four factors must be considered: (1) whether the entity
was created by the legislature; (2) whether its powers were specifically defined by the
legislature; (3) whether the property of the entity belongs to the public; and (4) whether
the entity’s functions are exclusively of a public character and performed solely for
public benefit.3 Further, all four factors must be present in order for a court to determine
that an entity is public.4 The Health Care Center is not an entity created by the
legislature, and its powers are not specifically defined by the legislature. If an entity fails
to meet the criteria of even one factor, it is not a public entity. Therefore, the Health
Care Center is not public.
Jurisprudence has made it clear that the mere fact that an entity is a private non-profit
does not mean that it can never be a public body for purposes of the Open Meetings
Law, nor does the fact that an entity receives public money mean that it is a public body
for purposes of the Open Meetings Law:
The legislative history surrounding the definition of the term “public body”
and the jurisprudence construing that term establish that the fact an entity
is set up as a private non-profit corporation is not dispositive of the
question of whether it is a public body for the purpose of the Open
Meetings Law. Moreover, the mere fact that an entity receives public
money does not make it a public body for the purpose of the Open
Meetings Law. Rather, there are a number of factors that must be
considered in determining whether an entity is subject to the Open
Meetings Law. Four factors courts have looked at in making this
determination are: (1) whether the entity performs a government function
or performs a function which, by law, is entrusted to other public bodies;
(2) whether the entity is funded by public money; (3) whether the entity
exercises policy-making, advisory, and administrative functions; and (4)
whether there is a connexity between the functions of the entity and the
functions of a particular “public body” identified in La. R.S. 42:13(A)(2).
3
State v. Smith, 357 So.2d 505, 507-08 (La.1978).
4
Property Insurance Association of Louisiana v. Theriot, 09-1152 (La.3/16/10), 31 So.3d 1012, 1015.

OPINION 13-0043
Representative Herbert B. Dixon
Page No. 3
Wayne v. Capital Area Legal Servs. Corp., 2011-1988 (La.App. 1 Cir.
9/26/12)(unpublished), 108 So. 3d 103, 114-15 writ denied, 2012-2343 (La.4/5/13), 110
So. 3d 1072.5
After the above-cited case was decided by the First Circuit Court of Appeals, the
Louisiana Supreme Court decided Louisiana High School Athletics Ass’n v. State.6 This
case considered the nature of the Louisiana High School Athletics Association
(“LHSAA”) and concluded this entity is not a “quasi-public agency or body” as defined
by La. R.S. 24:513(A).7 LHSAA is a non-profit corporation, organized by a group of
principals to promote and regulate interscholastic athletic competition.
In considering whether LHSAA falls within the definition of “public body” provided by La.
R.S. 42:13, the court reconsidered a previous decision regarding LHSAA,8 wherein
LHSAA was determined to be a public body under La. R.S. 42:13, reasoning that
LHSAA constitutes a “committee or subcommittee” of BESE or parish school boards
due the “connexity between the regulatory functions of the LHSAA and the regulatory
functions of a particular ‘public body’ found in R.S. 42:4.2(A)(2).”9 LHSAA, 107 So.3d at
606, citing Spain, 398 So.2d at 1390. Finding that the “connexity” factor is absent from
the statutory definition of a “public body,” LHSAA overruled the decision in Spain and
concluded that LHSAA is not a “public body” as defined by La. R.S. 42:13. The decision
went on to conclude that LHSAA cannot be considered a “quasi public agency or body”
as defined by La. R.S. 24:513(A)(1)(b)(v). Id. at 607.
Since LHSAA determined the “connexity” factor is not one which should be considered
in whether or not an entity is a “public body” under La. R.S. 42:13, we are left with three
remaining factors to consider: (1) whether the entity performs a government function or
performs a function which, by law, is entrusted to other public bodies; (2) whether the
entity is funded by public money; and (3) whether the entity exercises policy-making,
advisory, and administrative functions.
5 We note that the First Circuit remanded this case to the district court for an evidentiary hearing on the
issue of whether Capital Area Legal Services Corporation (“CALSC”) is a public body for the purpose of
the Open Meetings Law. This hearing was held on June 27, 2013, and the district court determined that
CALSC is not a public body.
6
2012-1471 (La. 1/29/13), 107 So.3d 583.
7 The relevance of this case to the instant opinion request is derived from the court’s analysis of whether
the LHSAA is subject to audit pursuant to La. R.S. 24:513(A)(1)(b)(v) which describes a quasi-public
agency or body as “[a]ny organization, either not-for-profit or for profit, which is subject to the open
meetings law and derives a portion of its income from payments received from any public agency or
body.” The Court determined LHSAA was not a quasi-public body after reaching the conclusion that it
was not required to comply with the Open Meetings Law.
8 Spain v LHSAA, 398 So.2d 1386 (La.1981).
9 La. R.S. 42:4.2 was redesignated as La. R.S. 42:13 by Act No. 861 of the 2010 Louisiana Legislative
Session.

OPINION 13-0043
Representative Herbert B. Dixon
Page No. 4
Your request indicates that Health Care Center provides health care to area residents,
particularly those who are economically disadvantaged. While this entity performs
services that governmental entities also provide by law, we understand that the Health
Care Center performs these services in addition to governmental entities which make
such services available to individuals in the same area. There is no evidence that
suggests the Health Care Center has been designated or funded as an agency by any
local entity to perform services which, by law, are entrusted to a public body. Further,
there is no evidence that suggests Health Care Center exercises policy-making,
advisory or administrative functions. Thus, it is the opinion of this office that the Health
Care Center is not a “public body” for purposes of the Open Meetings Law, and thus, is
not required to comply with the Open Meetings Law.
We hope that this opinion has adequately addressed the legal issues you have raised.
If our office can be of any further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.
With best regards,
JAMES D. “BUDDY” CALDWELL
